endorsements.title: Considerations for the regulation of generative AI-enabled medical devices (discussion paper)
endorsements.quote: assessment of risk in GenAI-enabled escalation functions should consider both directions of error.

endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)
endorsements.quote: Classify intended impact (noting whether the output will “touch” patients)

endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: Additional risk domains to consider include Financial, Legal, Operational, and Reputational risk.

commentary.bottom_line: No study supplied for this map tests whether rating AI functions as higher risk on the basis of verifiability, autonomy, patient contact, and harm severity changes how often errors reach patients. The recommendation rests on three endorsements, one from a regulatory discussion paper and two from CHAI frameworks, and none of them reports outcome data.

perspectives.view: Zero studies test the practice and zero studies document the hazard. Under GRADE conventions, certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence when no comparative or observational test exists. The three endorsements express expert agreement, but agreement among guidance documents does not measure whether risk tiering reduces patient harm.

The generative AI regulation discussion paper asks that risk assessment of escalation functions consider errors in both directions. The CHAI Assurance Standards Guide asks reviewers to note whether output will touch patients. The CHAI playbooks add financial, legal, operational, and reputational domains. Each source uses should language, and none of them is binding.

commentary.research_gap: No study compares risk review that weights verifiability, autonomy, patient contact, and harm severity against review that does not. Useful designs would track whether higher-tier ratings lead to added safeguards, and whether those safeguards reduce the number of uncaught errors that reach patients. A second gap is the absence of any supplied study that measures how often unverifiable or patient-facing AI errors go uncaught today.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested this practice, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Patients who have difficulty checking an AI output themselves may depend more on the human interception that risk tiering is meant to trigger, yet whether tiering protects these groups remains untested.
